claims.text: Reducing the Pt shell thickness in Pt/Cu core–shell nanoparticles enhances electronic coupling between the Cu core and Pt shell.
Stronger Cu–Pt electronic coupling downshifts the Pt d-band center.
A downshift of the Pt d-band center tunes the binding energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Optimally tuned intermediate binding maximizes ethanol-oxidation activity.
Optimally tuned intermediate binding maximizes ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Optimally tuned intermediate binding maximizes catalyst durability.
Complete ethanol oxidation involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
Commercial catalysts are typically Pt/Cu core–shell particles having uniformly thick Pt shells on preformed Cu cores.
Pt deposition time can be used to control Pt shell thickness on Cu cores.
In situ XPS or XAS can directly monitor electronic coupling and Pt d-band-center shifts during ethanol oxidation.
Thinner Pt shells permit a stronger electronic influence from the Cu core.
The Pt d-band-center shift adjusts the adsorption strength of oxygenated intermediates.
Adjusting adsorption strength through the d-band shift suppresses undesired overoxidation and side reactions.
Thicker Pt shells reduce the electronic effect of the Cu core and consequently give suboptimal catalytic performance.
Ethanol-oxidation activity and selectivity will exhibit a volcano-type dependence on Pt shell thickness.
An optimally thin Pt shell with the expected d-band shift will have higher turnover frequency and improved selectivity than much thinner or thicker shells.
Adsorption and desorption energetics of intermediates govern ethanol-oxidation kinetics under the stated electrochemical regime.
Extreme potentials, temperatures, or environments can significantly alter catalyst surface chemistry or morphology and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Changing Pt deposition conditions may introduce confounding morphological or compositional changes.
